tasks.name: Use greedy choices only when they are provably safe
Design dynamic programming state and transitions

concepts.name: Backtracking choose/explore/undo
concepts.description: Explore a decision tree by making one choice, recursively exploring consequences, and undoing that choice before trying alternatives.

concepts.name: Backtracking state contract
concepts.description: Maintain only the partial candidate and constraint state needed to decide what choices remain valid.

concepts.name: Backtracking pruning
concepts.description: Stop exploring a partial candidate as soon as a constraint proves no completion below it can succeed.

concepts.name: Greedy safe-choice reasoning
concepts.description: Choose the locally preferred option only when a proof shows some optimal solution can start with that choice.

concepts.name: Greedy interval scheduling
concepts.description: Maximize the number of non-overlapping intervals by repeatedly choosing the compatible interval with earliest finish time.

concepts.name: Greedy versus DP discrimination
concepts.description: Distinguish problems with a provably safe irreversible local choice from problems that require comparing multiple future consequences.

concepts.name: DP state and transition
concepts.description: Define a state that captures the information future decisions need, then express that state from smaller states.

concepts.name: Memoization and tabulation
concepts.description: Compute overlapping subproblems once, either top-down on demand or bottom-up in dependency order.

concepts.name: Sequence and resource DP
concepts.description: Use DP for sequence alignment/editing and bounded resource-allocation problems when choices interact through remaining position or capacity.

questions.prompt: A test generator chooses six config parameters. Constraints can fail only after several choices, and invalid partial configs can often be rejected early. It must emit every valid config. Which design best exploits that structure?
questions.explanation: The solution is built from sequential choices, multiple alternatives must be explored, and partial assignments can become invalid. Backtracking matches that decision-tree structure.
hints: You need all valid combinations, not one locally preferred choice.

error_codes.description: The selected strategy does not match constrained enumeration over multiple alternative choices.

choice_feedback.backtrack: Correct: choose, explore, undo, then try the sibling choice.
choice_feedback.greedy: A single irreversible local choice can miss valid configurations.
choice_feedback.binary: There is no monotonic ordered answer domain.
choice_feedback.heap: Priority ordering does not enumerate constrained combinations.

choices.label: Build one partial config at a time, prune impossible branches, undo, and try siblings
Pick the first currently valid option for each parameter and never revisit earlier choices
Generate the full Cartesian product first, then filter every complete config
Memoize only by parameter index even though different partial constraints remain active

questions.prompt: Order one backtracking branch before trying its sibling.
questions.explanation: Choose, mutate state, explore, undo, then try the next candidate. Undo must happen before the sibling branch.
hints: Sibling branches should begin from the same parent state.

error_codes.description: The backtracking branch lifecycle is out of order.

items.label: Choose candidate A
Apply A to mutable state
Explore descendants under A
Undo A
Try candidate B

questions.prompt: A backtracker appends a choice to `chosen`, recursively explores, and then immediately tries the next sibling without removing the prior choice. Flag the bug.
questions.explanation: The prior branch's mutable state leaks into the sibling branch. The algorithm must restore state—such as popping the appended choice—before trying the next sibling.
hints: Sibling branches must start from the same parent partial candidate.

error_codes.description: The missing state restoration was not identified.
A valid choose/explore step was incorrectly flagged.

elements.label: Leave the candidate in mutable state before exploring the next sibling

questions.prompt: A deployment configuration may request at most 16 GiB. All remaining component memory sizes are non-negative. A partial branch already requests 18 GiB. What is the correct action?
questions.explanation: The branch already violates a hard upper bound and future choices cannot reduce usage, so no completion can become valid. Prune it immediately.
hints: Can any later non-negative addition reduce 18 GiB to at most 16 GiB?

error_codes.description: The selected action does not use the proven hard-bound failure correctly.

choice_feedback.prune: Correct: the branch is provably impossible.
choice_feedback.continue: Continuing explores states that cannot satisfy the hard bound.
choice_feedback.greedy: Choosing the smallest remaining item still cannot repair an already-exceeded upper bound.
choice_feedback.restart: Restarting the entire search is unnecessary; only this branch is invalid.

choices.label: Prune this branch now
Continue all remaining choices before deciding
Force the smallest remaining item and keep going
Discard the entire search and restart from the root

questions.prompt: A config search has already selected some components. Which facts are strong enough to delete the entire remaining branch without risking a valid/better answer?
questions.explanation: Pruning requires proof that no completion below the partial state can succeed or improve enough. A branch may be tried later or ordered last without being pruned if it merely looks unpromising.
hints: A safe prune must preserve correctness.

error_codes.description: A correctness-preserving prune condition was missed.
A heuristic or cost concern was incorrectly treated as proof of impossibility.

evidence.label: The partial assignment already violates a required constraint that later choices cannot repair
A proven upper/lower bound shows this branch cannot beat the current best
The branch looks unlikely based only on intuition
The branch is expensive to evaluate

questions.prompt: A feature-assignment solver mutates shared branch state. Classify each behavior as safe backtracking discipline or a correctness risk.
questions.explanation: Correct backtracking restores sibling state and prunes only with proof. Branch ordering heuristics are fine, but they must not silently delete possible solutions.
hints: Separate exploration order from correctness-preserving elimination.

error_codes.description: At least one backtracking behavior was classified incorrectly.
At least one backtracking behavior was not classified.

items.label: Undo mutable state before the sibling branch
Prune after a hard constraint proves impossibility
Discard a branch because it merely looks unlikely
Copy a complete mutable solution before later backtracking changes it

questions.prompt: A test-config generator must explore alternatives without leaking state between siblings. Reconstruct the branch lifecycle.
questions.explanation: The reusable skeleton checks completion/invalidity, iterates candidate choices, applies one, explores recursively, and restores state before the next sibling.
hints: State restoration belongs before trying another sibling.

error_codes.description: At least one backtracking skeleton step was left empty.
At least one backtracking skeleton step was misplaced.
A state-leaking step was selected.
A required backtracking step was omitted.

pieces.label: Check complete solution / provably invalid partial state
Keep all prior sibling state permanently

questions.prompt: A policy compiler must enumerate all valid rule assignments under mutual-exclusion and prerequisite constraints, and should abandon impossible partial assignments early. Which design best matches?
questions.explanation: This is constrained combinatorial enumeration: backtracking explores rule assignments, and safe constraint checks prune impossible partial assignments.

error_codes.description: The selected strategy does not match complete constrained assignment search.

choice_feedback.bt: Correct: it explores all relevant assignments while pruning proven-impossible branches.
choice_feedback.greedy: An irreversible local rule choice can miss valid assignments.
choice_feedback.sort: Sorting rules does not enumerate compatibility assignments.
choice_feedback.bfs: Graph BFS is not the core decision structure here.

choices.label: Backtracking with incremental constraint checks and pruning
Choose one currently compatible rule at each step and never revisit that choice
Generate every complete assignment first, then run the constraint checker afterward
Cache only by the number of assigned rules, ignoring which constraints are active

questions.prompt: A scheduler wants to permanently commit to one locally preferred job without exploring alternatives later. What evidence would justify making that irreversible choice?
questions.explanation: A greedy choice needs a safety proof, such as showing an optimal solution can be exchanged to use that choice without worsening the objective.
hints: Performance on a few examples is not a correctness proof.

error_codes.description: The selected evidence does not establish greedy-choice correctness.

choice_feedback.proof: Correct: a safety/exchange argument justifies permanent commitment.
choice_feedback.fast: Fast runtime does not imply optimality.
choice_feedback.examples: Passing examples is evidence but not a general proof.
choice_feedback.local: Being locally largest/smallest is not sufficient by itself.

choices.label: A correctness argument showing some optimal schedule can always begin with that choice
The rule can be implemented in O(n log n)
The rule beats brute force on the sample inputs tested so far
The chosen job has the best local metric right now, but no exchange/safety argument

questions.prompt: One test lab can run one booking at a time. Every accepted booking has equal value, and the objective is maximum booking count. Which local rule has the right future-space argument?
questions.explanation: Choose the compatible booking with earliest finish time. That leaves at least as much remaining time as any alternative first compatible booking.
hints: The objective is number of bookings, not total duration or value.

error_codes.description: The selected rule is not the proven greedy rule for maximizing the number of non-overlapping intervals.

choice_feedback.finish: Correct: earliest finish is the safe choice for maximum interval count.
choice_feedback.short: Shortest duration is not generally equivalent to earliest finish.
choice_feedback.start: Earliest start can occupy a long interval and block many later bookings.
choice_feedback.value: All bookings have equal value here; highest value is not the objective.

choices.label: Choose the compatible booking that finishes earliest
Choose the compatible booking with the shortest duration
Choose the compatible booking that starts earliest
Choose the compatible booking leaving the smallest immediate idle gap

questions.prompt: One test lab wants to accept the maximum number of equal-value non-overlapping bookings. Order the earliest-finish scheduling process.
questions.explanation: Sort by finish time, take the earliest-finishing compatible interval, then continue scanning for the next interval that starts after the selected finish.
hints: The sort key is finish time.

error_codes.description: The interval-scheduling greedy process is out of order.

items.label: Sort intervals by increasing finish time
Accept the earliest-finishing interval
Scan remaining intervals in that order
Accept an interval when its start is compatible with the last accepted finish

questions.prompt: A team reuses earliest-finish interval scheduling for jobs that now have DIFFERENT PROFITS and wants maximum total profit. Flag the reasoning error.
questions.explanation: Earliest finish is optimal for maximum COUNT of equal-value non-overlapping intervals, not maximum total profit. Weighted interval scheduling changes the objective and requires different reasoning, typically DP.
hints: The objective changed from count to weighted value.

error_codes.description: The invalid transfer of the unweighted greedy proof to weighted profit was not identified.
A valid part of the weighted scheduling problem statement was incorrectly flagged.

elements.label: Represent each job as an interval with a finish time
Assume earliest finish still maximizes total profit merely because it maximizes interval count
Include job profit in the objective

questions.prompt: A build cache has capacity 10. A=(size 10, save 10 min), B=(5,9), C=(5,9). Why does 'take the single highest-saving artifact first' fail?
questions.explanation: The greedy rule picks A for value 10, but B+C fit together and save 18 minutes. A small counterexample disproves the local-choice rule for indivisible bounded selection.
hints: Compare A alone with the combination B+C.

error_codes.description: The selected explanation does not identify the counterexample to the greedy rule.

choice_feedback.combo: Correct: a combination of individually smaller choices is better.
choice_feedback.capacity: Capacity is exactly why combinations interact; it does not make greedy safe.
choice_feedback.sort: Sorting does not change the counterexample.
choice_feedback.equal: The artifacts do not have equal values.

choices.label: B+C fit together and save 18 minutes, so the locally best single item blocks a better combination
A uses the whole capacity, so no second item can be considered; that by itself does not prove optimality
Sorting by value descending preserves the same bad first choice A
Using value/size ratio also needs a correctness argument for indivisible 0/1 choices

questions.prompt: A scheduler/cache optimizer has four optimization shapes. Classify which ones support a proof-backed irreversible choice versus which need future trade-offs kept in state.
questions.explanation: Greedy is appropriate when a safe local commitment is provable. DP is the stronger clue when indivisible choices consume shared resources or weighted future alternatives must be compared.
hints: Ask whether one local choice can be committed without future regret.

error_codes.description: At least one optimization shape was matched to the wrong reasoning family.
At least one optimization shape was not classified.

items.label: Maximum number of equal-value non-overlapping intervals
Maximum total value of non-overlapping weighted intervals
Indivisible items with value under a capacity limit
A local choice has an exchange proof showing it is always safe

questions.prompt: Which evidence supports an earliest-finish greedy rule for maximum COUNT of non-overlapping intervals?
questions.explanation: The earliest-finishing compatible interval leaves no less remaining time than another compatible first interval, and the objective counts each selected interval equally.
hints: The proof depends on both the objective and the remaining-time argument.

error_codes.description: Part of the interval-scheduling greedy argument was missed.
A property not required by the earliest-finish proof was selected.

evidence.label: Each accepted interval contributes the same unit count to the objective
Earlier finish leaves at least as much remaining timeline for future compatible intervals
Intervals can have arbitrary profit and the objective is maximum total profit
The shortest-duration interval is always the earliest-finishing interval

questions.prompt: A CI runner can execute one job at a time during a fixed maintenance window. Every candidate job counts equally and jobs cannot overlap. The goal is to complete as many jobs as possible. Which rule fits?
questions.explanation: This is the classic maximum-cardinality interval scheduling objective, so earliest compatible finish is the correct greedy rule.

error_codes.description: The selected rule is not the proven greedy rule for maximum equal-value interval count.

choice_feedback.finish: Correct: maximum equal-value interval count uses earliest finish.
choice_feedback.start: Earliest start can block many later jobs.
choice_feedback.long: Longest duration is contrary to the goal of fitting many jobs.
choice_feedback.profit: The problem states every job counts equally.

choices.label: Sort by finish time and repeatedly accept the next compatible job
Always accept the earliest-starting job
Always accept the longest-duration job
Assign arbitrary profits and choose the largest first

questions.prompt: For indivisible cache artifacts processed from index `i` onward with a remaining byte budget, which state most directly captures the future decision problem?
questions.explanation: The future depends on which artifacts remain and how much capacity remains, so `(i, remaining_capacity)` is a sufficient state.
hints: Two histories should be equivalent if all future choices have the same consequences.

error_codes.description: The selected state does not minimally capture the future cache-selection subproblem.

choice_feedback.state: Correct: index and remaining capacity determine future options.
choice_feedback.value: Current accumulated value alone does not say which items/capacity remain.
choice_feedback.history: The full history is more information than future decisions need.
choice_feedback.last: The last chosen artifact alone is insufficient.

choices.label: `(i, remaining_capacity)`
Only total value accumulated so far
The full list of every prior choice as the DP key
Only the last artifact chosen

questions.prompt: State `best(i, remaining)` means maximum value obtainable from items `i..end`. Item i has size s and value v. If `s <= remaining`, which transition is correct for 0/1 selection?
questions.explanation: The item is indivisible and usable at most once, so compare skipping it with taking it and moving to i+1 with reduced capacity.
hints: Both branches move to the next item; only the take branch reduces capacity.

error_codes.description: The selected transition does not model mutually exclusive take/skip choices for a 0/1 item.

choice_feedback.correct: Correct: `max(skip, take)` compares both future consequences.
choice_feedback.repeat: Keeping i after taking allows the same 0/1 item to be reused.
choice_feedback.greedy: Taking whenever it fits is not generally optimal.
choice_feedback.sum: Adding both take and skip values double-counts mutually exclusive decisions.

choices.label: `max(best(i+1, remaining), v + best(i+1, remaining-s))`
`v + best(i, remaining-s)` for every fitting item
Always take item i whenever it fits
Add the skip result and take result together

questions.prompt: A recursive cache optimizer repeatedly reaches the same `(item_index, remaining_capacity)` states. You want to keep the recursive structure and compute only states that are actually reached. What change fits?
questions.explanation: Memoization caches each state result and reuses it when the same state is reached again.
hints: The repeated work is identical subproblem evaluation.

error_codes.description: The selected change does not eliminate repeated evaluation of identical DP states.

choice_feedback.memo: Correct: cache results by DP state.
choice_feedback.sort: Sorting states does not stop recursive recomputation by itself.
choice_feedback.greedy: Changing to greedy changes the algorithm and may lose optimality.
choice_feedback.copy: Copying the input does not reuse state answers.

choices.label: Memoize results by the full `(item_index, remaining_capacity)` state
Cache only by `item_index`, treating different remaining capacities as the same state
Keep the recursion unchanged but cache by the current accumulated value
Recompute identical states but copy the item list on every call

questions.prompt: Two engineers implement the same DP recurrence differently. Match each implementation behavior to top-down memoization or bottom-up tabulation.
questions.explanation: Memoization is top-down and demand-driven through recursive calls; tabulation explicitly fills states bottom-up in dependency order.
hints: Ask whether recursion requests states on demand or a table is filled deliberately.

error_codes.description: At least one DP computation style was classified incorrectly.
At least one DP computation style was not classified.

items.label: Recursive function checks a cache before computing a state
Iterate states in dependency order from base cases upward
Compute only states reached by recursive calls
Fill an explicit DP table row by row

questions.prompt: Two partial histories have the same proposed DP state, but one still has 3 GiB capacity and the other has 8 GiB. Future choices differ. Flag the state-design mistake.
questions.explanation: A valid DP state must make histories with the same state future-equivalent. Omitting remaining capacity merges subproblems with different feasible futures.
hints: Would the same future artifacts fit in both histories?

error_codes.description: The missing capacity state dimension was not identified.
A valid DP design element was incorrectly flagged.

elements.label: Track which item index is next
Treat states with different remaining capacities as identical
Define a base case after the last item

questions.prompt: A config-diff tool needs minimum insert/delete/replace edits between two strings. Which state preserves the future-relevant position in both strings?
questions.explanation: A two-sequence position state such as `(i, j)` represents the remaining suffixes. A mismatch can compare several edit consequences, which is a classic DP shape.
hints: The future depends on positions in both sequences.

error_codes.description: The selected approach does not model interacting sequence-edit decisions correctly.

choice_feedback.ij: Correct: positions in both sequences identify the subproblem.
choice_feedback.greedy: Fixing the first mismatch greedily can block a globally cheaper edit sequence.
choice_feedback.heap: Priority ordering alone does not model the two suffix positions.
choice_feedback.hash: Exact membership state does not capture alignment choices.

choices.label: DP state `(i,j)` for the remaining suffixes of both strings
Only the first mismatch position; always replace immediately
State `i` in the first string only, ignoring position in the second
Character-frequency map, which loses order/alignment

questions.prompt: A recursive optimizer branches on choices. Which observations tell you that caching/reusing subproblem results may be the right next step?
questions.explanation: DP is a strong fit when the problem decomposes into smaller states, the same states recur, and each state's answer can be expressed from dependent smaller states.
hints: Look for reusable subproblems and a state recurrence.

error_codes.description: A strong dynamic-programming clue was missed.
A property that does not itself justify DP was selected.

evidence.label: Different decision histories reach the same future subproblem
A state can be expressed from smaller/dependent states
Every subproblem is guaranteed to occur exactly once

questions.prompt: A build cache can hold 12 GiB. Each artifact is indivisible and has a size plus an estimated rebuild-time saving. You need the set with maximum total saving that fits. Which approach best matches the decision structure?
questions.explanation: This is a 0/1 resource-allocation shape: each artifact is taken or skipped once, choices share a remaining-capacity constraint, and greedy value/ratio rules are not generally safe.

error_codes.description: The selected approach does not correctly model interacting indivisible choices under a capacity constraint.

choice_feedback.dp: Correct: item index plus remaining capacity captures the reusable future subproblem.
choice_feedback.greedy: Highest value or ratio first is not generally optimal for indivisible 0/1 choices.
choice_feedback.sort: Sorting alone does not resolve interacting capacity choices.
choice_feedback.bfs: Unweighted graph distance is not the optimization structure.

choices.label: Dynamic programming over `(artifact_index, remaining_capacity)`
Always take the highest-saving artifact that still fits
Sort by artifact name and take a prefix
Run BFS over artifact IDs without modeling capacity
